section: 2 The rule for scoring sequential forecasts
text:
2 The rule for scoring sequential forecasts
A forecast may use only information available before kickoff, including information used to set tuning parameters. Sequential updates alone do not prevent leakage if hyperparameters were fitted using future games. Here we fix illustrative hyperparameters in advance rather than use the stored full-period Stan fit for forecast scoring. The 2022 season supplies initial ratings and the baseline home-win rate. We score 2023 and 2024 games with decisive outcomes. This targets performance among decisive games. A full outcome model would include ties explicitly.

baseline_home_rate <- with(subset(nfl, season == 2022 & tie == 0), mean(home_win))

elo <- run_elo(nfl, k = 20, home_advantage = 55, margin_multiplier = TRUE)
kalman <- kalman_ratings(
  nfl,
  sigma_obs = 13, sigma_week = 1.2,
  sigma_season = 4, rho = 0.6,
  home_advantage = 2, initial_sd = 6
)

# Rolling ridge: before each week, refit on the current season's earlier games.
rolling_ridge <- nfl %>%
  mutate(ridge_margin = NA_real_)
for (s in unique(nfl$season)) {
  for (w in sort(unique(nfl$week[nfl$season == s]))) {
    rows <- which(nfl$season == s & nfl$week == w)
    history <- nfl %>% filter(season == s, week < w)
    if (nrow(history) < 16) {
      rolling_ridge$ridge_margin[rows] <- 2 * (1 - nfl$neutral_site[rows])
    } else {
      fit <- ridge_ratings(history, lambda = 7)
      rolling_ridge$ridge_margin[rows] <- fit$home_advantage * (1 - nfl$neutral_site[rows]) +
        fit$ratings[nfl$home_team[rows]] - fit$ratings[nfl$away_team[rows]]
    }
  }
}

forecasts <- nfl %>%
  select(game_id, season, week, home_team, away_team, margin, home_win, tie, spread_line, home_moneyline, away_moneyline) %>%
  left_join(elo$games %>% select(game_id, elo_prob = home_prob), by = "game_id") %>%
  left_join(kalman$predictions %>% select(game_id, kalman_margin = predicted_margin, kalman_prob = home_prob), by = "game_id") %>%
  left_join(rolling_ridge %>% select(game_id, ridge_margin), by = "game_id") %>%
  mutate(
    ridge_prob = pnorm(ridge_margin / 13),
    market_prob = remove_vig(moneyline_to_probability(home_moneyline), moneyline_to_probability(away_moneyline))[, 1],
    spread_prob = pnorm(spread_line / 13.5)
  ) %>%
  filter(season >= 2023, tie == 0, !is.na(market_prob))

3 The market as a benchmark
A moneyline of −150-150 means a bettor risks 150 to win 100; a moneyline of +130+130 means risking 100 wins 130. The implied probabilities are
pimplied={|M||M|+100,M<0,100M+100,M>0.
p_{\text{implied}}=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{|M|}{|M|+100}, & M<0,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{100}{M+100}, & M>0.
\end{cases}

The two sides of a game imply probabilities that sum to more than one. The excess is the bookmaker’s margin, called the vig or hold, and dividing each implied probability by the sum removes it.

    hold = implied_home + implied_away - 1,

4.1 Calibration

calibration <- bind_rows(
  forecasts %>% transmute(model = "Elo", probability = elo_prob, home_win),
  forecasts %>% transmute(model = "Kalman filter", probability = kalman_prob, home_win),
  forecasts %>% transmute(model = "market (moneyline)", probability = market_prob, home_win)
) %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(probability, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1), include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(model, bin) %>%
  summarize(mean_forecast = mean(probability), observed = mean(home_win), games = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(games >= 10)

ggplot(calibration, aes(mean_forecast, observed, color = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = games)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +

section: 5 Break-even, expected value, and the difficulty of beating the market
text:
5 Break-even, expected value, and the difficulty of beating the market
A bet at decimal odds oo (American +M+M converts to o=1+M/100o=1+M/100; −M-M converts to o=1+100/Mo=1+100/M) returns oo per unit staked if it wins. If the true probability is pp, the expected profit per unit is
EV=po−1,
\text{EV}=p\,o-1,

and the bet breaks even at p*=1/op^{*}=1/o, which is exactly the implied probability before the vig is removed. To profit, a model’s probability must exceed the implied probability of the bettor’s side, which already includes the hold, and it must do so reliably.

edges <- forecasts %>%
  mutate(
    odds_home = ifelse(home_moneyline > 0, 1 + home_moneyline / 100, 1 + 100 / abs(home_moneyline)),
    odds_away = ifelse(away_moneyline > 0, 1 + away_moneyline / 100, 1 + 100 / abs(away_moneyline)),
    ev_home = kalman_prob * odds_home - 1,
    ev_away = (1 - kalman_prob) * odds_away - 1,
    bet = case_when(ev_home > 0.05 ~ "home", ev_away > 0.05 ~ "away", TRUE ~ "none"),
    profit = case_when(
      bet == "home" ~ ifelse(home_win == 1, odds_home - 1, -1),
      bet == "away" ~ ifelse(home_win == 0, odds_away - 1, -1),
      TRUE ~ 0
    )
  )

edges %>%
  filter(bet != "none") %>%
  summarize(
    bets = n(),
    win_rate = mean(profit > 0),
    total_profit_per_unit_staked = sum(profit) / n(),
    mean_model_edge = mean(pmax(ev_home, ev_away))
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

First, an apparent edge on one season of games is within noise; a return of a few percent on a few hundred bets has a standard error of several percent. Second, the Kelly criterion f*=(po−1)/(o−1)f^{*}=(po-1)/(o-1) gives the stake fraction that maximizes long-run growth if pp is correct; with an overconfident model it produces ruin faster than flat betting.

title: 5.6 Evaluating and Communicating Team Ratings
text:
9 Key takeaways

Score forecasts made only with pregame information, after a warm-up period, and exclude outcomes the forecast cannot express.
Moneylines convert to probabilities; remove the hold before comparing with a model.
The market beats results-only models; the state-space model is the best of those models and the rolling static model the worst.
Apparent betting edges from a results-only model do not survive the hold; treat market log loss as the bar to clear.
Report rankings as rank probabilities and state scale, uncertainty, timing, and blind spots.

title: 5.4 Goals as Counts: A Bayesian Multilevel Poisson Model
text:
2 The model
Each match produces two counts. Let YmHY_{m}^{H} and YmAY_{m}^{A} be the home and away goals in match mm between home team ii and away team jj. The Poisson model (Maher, 1982) is
YmH∼Poisson(λmH),log⁡λmH=μ+β+ai+dj,
Y_m^{H}\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda_m^{H}),
\qquad
\log\lambda_m^{H}=\mu+\beta+a_i+d_j,

YmA∼Poisson(λmA),log⁡λmA=μ+aj+di,
Y_m^{A}\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda_m^{A}),
\qquad
\log\lambda_m^{A}=\mu+a_j+d_i,

where μ\mu is the log of the baseline scoring rate, β\beta is the home advantage on the log scale, aa is a team’s attack effect, and dd is the effect of facing that team’s defense. A positive djd_j means opponents score more against team jj; a good defense has a negative dd. Home and away goals are treated as independent given the rates.
On the count scale, eβe^{\beta} multiplies the home team’s expected goals and eaie^{a_i} multiplies goals for team ii’s attack. The log link turns the additive model into a multiplicative one, which is what keeps expected goals positive.

2.1 The multilevel layer
The attack and defense effects are crossed random effects, exactly as in Lecture 4:
ai∼N(0,τa2),dj∼N(0,τd2).
a_i\sim N(0,\tau_a^2),
\qquad
d_j\sim N(0,\tau_d^2).

With only 38 matches per team, shrinkage matters. A team that scored freely in its first ten matches is pulled toward the league until the evidence accumulates.


2.2 The data in long form
Each match becomes two rows, one per team’s attack.

3 The Bayesian fit
The model was fitted with rstanarm::stan_glmer() and stored in data/team_results.rds. The call and the priors were:

library(rstanarm)

poisson_fit <- stan_glmer(
  goals ~ home + (1 | attack) + (1 | defense),
  data = goals_long,
  family = poisson(),
  prior_intercept = normal(0, 1),
  prior = normal(0, 1),
  prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.5),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  seed = 431
)

rstanarm applies prior_intercept after centering fixed predictors. With h‾=0.5\bar h=0.5, the centered intercept is αc=μ+h‾β\alpha_c=\mu+\bar h\beta. The specified priors are αc∼N(0,1)\alpha_c\sim N(0,1) and β∼N(0,1)\beta\sim N(0,1) independently, so the prior on the raw away baseline μ=αc−h‾β\mu=\alpha_c-\bar h\beta is induced rather than independent. For these one-dimensional random-effect blocks, decov(scale = 0.5) gives each standard deviation a gamma prior with shape 1 and scale 0.5. Check poisson$prior_summary for the fitted parameterization.

text:
5 Posterior predictive checks
A Bayesian model can generate data. If simulated seasons look unlike the real one in some respect, the model is missing something. The stored replications object holds 500 simulated seasons, one per posterior draw, each with the same fixtures.

replications <- poisson$replications
dim(replications)

[1] 500 760



5.1 Goal counts

goal_check <- lapply(0:7, function(g) {
  replicated <- rowMeans(replications == g)
  data.frame(
    goals = g,
    observed = mean(goals_long$goals == g),
    predicted = mean(replicated),
    lower = quantile(replicated, 0.05),
    upper = quantile(replicated, 0.95)
  )
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

ggplot(goal_check, aes(goals)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = observed), fill = "#03a9e6", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = predicted), size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Goals by one team", y = "Proportion of team-matches") +
  theme_minimal()




Observed distribution of goals per team-match (bars) against the posterior predictive distribution (points with 90% bands).






5.2 Draws, high scores, and dispersion
Three summary statistics test different aspects of the model: the share of drawn matches tests the independence assumption at low scores, the maximum goals scored by one team in one match tests the tail, and the variance-to-mean ratio tests for overdispersion.

home_rows <- which(goals_long$home == 1)
away_candidates <- which(goals_long$home == 0)

6 Match probabilities
For a fixture between home team ii and away team jj, each posterior draw gives a pair of rates (λH,λA)(\lambda^H,\lambda^A). Under independence, the probability of the score (h,a)(h,a) is the product of two Poisson probabilities, and the outcome probabilities are sums over the score grid:
P(home win)=∑h>ae−λH(λH)hh!⋅e−λA(λA)aa!,
P(\text{home win})=\sum_{h>a}\frac{e^{-\lambda^H}(\lambda^H)^h}{h!}\cdot\frac{e^{-\lambda^A}(\lambda^A)^a}{a!},

with the draw and away-win probabilities defined by h=ah=a and h<ah<a. Averaging over posterior draws integrates out the uncertainty in the rates.

draw_index <- sample(nrow(poisson$attack_draws), 200)

  a <- epl_2324$away_team[[m]]

    poisson$attack_draws[draw_index, h] + poisson$defense_draws[draw_index, a])
  lambda_away <- exp(poisson$intercept_draws[draw_index] +
    poisson$attack_draws[draw_index, a] + poisson$defense_draws[draw_index, h])
  rowMeans(mapply(poisson_match_probabilities, lambda_home, lambda_away))
}))

text:
8 Limitations and extensions

Independence. Home and away goals are modeled as independent. Empirically there is mild dependence at low scores; Dixon and Coles (1997) multiply the probability of the four lowest scorelines (0-0, 1-0, 0-1, 1-1) by a correction with one parameter ρ\rho, which raises the draw probability. Bivariate Poisson models add a shared component instead.
Overdispersion. Goal counts are close to Poisson, so a negative binomial is rarely needed for team totals. Corners, shots, or fouls are typically overdispersed.
Time. Strength changes within a season through injuries, transfers, and form. Dixon and Coles weight past matches by e−ξte^{-\xi t}; Tutorial 5.5 lets strength evolve explicitly.
Expected goals. Replacing goals with expected goals as the response reduces noise but changes the target from what happened to what the chances were worth.

9 Practice

A team has attack effect 0.25 and faces a defense with effect −0.15-0.15 at home, with μ=0.2\mu=0.2 and β=0.2\beta=0.2. What is its expected goal count?
Why is the defense effect written with a positive sign in the linear predictor?
Name one posterior predictive check that would detect a failure of the independence assumption and one that would not.
Why should match probabilities be averaged over posterior draws rather than computed from the posterior means of the rates?







TipShow answers






exp⁡(0.2+0.2+0.25−0.15)=e0.5≈1.65\exp(0.2+0.2+0.25-0.15)=e^{0.5}\approx1.65 goals.
It is the effect of facing that defense on the opponent’s scoring rate; a good defense has a negative value. The sign is a convention that matches the (1 | defense) term.
The draw share can detect it; the distribution of goals per team cannot, because independence concerns the joint distribution of the two counts.
The outcome probabilities are nonlinear in the rates, so the average of the probabilities is not the probability at the average rates; averaging over draws also carries the uncertainty in the effects into the forecast.

2 The design matrix
Each game gg contributes one row. Let xgj=+1x_{gj}=+1 if team jj is the home team, −1-1 if it is the away team, and 00 otherwise, and let hg=1h_g=1 unless the game was played at a neutral site. The margin model is
yg=αhg+∑jxgjθj+εg=αhg+θhome(g)−θaway(g)+εg,εg∼N(0,σ2).
y_g=\alpha h_g+\sum_{j}x_{gj}\theta_j+\varepsilon_g
=\alpha h_g+\theta_{\text{home}(g)}-\theta_{\text{away}(g)}+\varepsilon_g,
\qquad
\varepsilon_g\sim N(0,\sigma^2).

This is the adjusted plus-minus design of Lecture 4 with teams in place of players and exactly one team on each side.

X <- build_design_matrix(games_2023)
dim(X)

[1] 272  32

X[1:4, 1:8]

[1,]   0   0   0   0   0   0   0   0
[2,]  -1   0   0   0   0   0   0   0
[3,]   0   1   0   0  -1   0   0   0
[4,]   0   0   0   0   0   0  -1   1


Every row sums to zero, so the columns are linearly dependent and X𝖳XX^{\mathsf T}X is singular. Adding a constant to every θj\theta_j leaves every θhome−θaway\theta_{\text{home}}-\theta_{\text{away}} unchanged. Only differences between ratings are identified. Two standard fixes are to drop one team’s column (a reference team) or to impose ∑jθj=0\sum_j\theta_j=0. The functions below fit with a reference team and then recenter, which is equivalent.

section: 4 A Gaussian prior on the ratings
text:
4 A Gaussian prior on the ratings
Least squares treats every rating as a free parameter. A better assumption is that ratings come from a population: most teams are near average and a few are far from it. Write
θj∼N(0,τ2),
\theta_j\sim N(0,\tau^2),

which, as Lecture 4 showed, makes the posterior mode the ridge estimator
𝜽̂=(X𝖳X+λI)−1X𝖳(𝒚−α̂𝒉),λ=σ2τ2.
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=\left(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I\right)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\left(\mathbf y-\hat\alpha\mathbf h\right),
\qquad
\lambda=\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}.







NoteMathematical details: why subtract estimated home advantage?





The model and independent Gaussian prior are
𝒚=α𝒉+X𝜽+𝜺,𝜺∼N(𝟎,σ2I),𝜽∼N(𝟎,τ2I).
\mathbf y=\alpha\mathbf h+X\boldsymbol\theta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim N(\mathbf0,\sigma^2I),
\qquad \boldsymbol\theta\sim N(\mathbf0,\tau^2I).

Here each margin is home minus away, so hg=1h_g=1 for a home venue and hg=0h_g=0 at a neutral site. With a flat prior on α\alpha and fixed positive variances, maximizing the posterior is equivalent to minimizing
Q(𝜽,α)=∥𝒚−α𝒉−X𝜽∥2+λ∥𝜽∥2,λ=σ2/τ2.
Q(\boldsymbol\theta,\alpha)
=\|\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h-X\boldsymbol\theta\|^2
+\lambda\|\boldsymbol\theta\|^2,
\qquad \lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2.

Differentiating with respect to the ratings gives
−2X𝖳(𝒚−α𝒉−X𝜽)+2λ𝜽=𝟎.
-2X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h-X\boldsymbol\theta)
+2\lambda\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf0.

If α\alpha were known, the solution would use 𝒚−α𝒉\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h. At the joint optimum, its value is α̂\hat\alpha, giving
𝜽̂=(X𝖳X+λI)−1X𝖳(𝒚−α̂𝒉).
\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}
=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I)^{-1}
X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-\hat\alpha\mathbf h).

The hat means that home advantage is estimated. It introduces no extra approximation into this equation. The two estimates satisfy simultaneous equations; for example, when 𝒉𝖳𝒉>0\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h>0,
α̂=𝒉𝖳(𝒚−X𝜽̂)𝒉𝖳𝒉.
\hat\alpha=\frac{\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-X\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})}
{\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}\mathbf h}.




The penalty also solves the identification problem: pulling every rating toward zero pins down the constant that least squares could not.






NoteMathematical details: rating levels and the last team’s rating





Because X𝟏=𝟎X\mathbf1=\mathbf0, adding a constant to all ratings leaves predicted margins unchanged. If we impose the zero-sum convention, the last rating satisfies
θJ=−∑j=1J−1θj.
\theta_J=-\sum_{j=1}^{J-1}\theta_j.

This is a constraint defining the baseline, not another observation. With the independent zero-centered Gaussian prior used above, the ridge mode automatically has zero sum: multiply its normal equations by 𝟏𝖳\mathbf1^{\mathsf T} to obtain λ𝟏𝖳𝜽̂=0\lambda\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=0. Individual prior or posterior draws need not sum to zero unless explicitly centered or constrained. An explicitly constrained Gaussian prior has dependent ratings, so it should not be confused with independent priors on all JJ ratings.



For a team with GG games against average opponents, the ridge estimate is approximately
θ̂j≈GG+λm‾j,
\hat\theta_j\approx\frac{G}{G+\lambda}\,\bar m_j,

where m‾j\bar m_j is its adjusted average margin. With σ=13\sigma=13 and τ=5\tau=5, λ≈6.8\lambda\approx6.8, and a 17-game season keeps about 17/23.8≈71%17/23.8\approx71\% of the observed deviation.






NoteMathematical details: ridge shrinkage






4.1 Deriving the approximation for one team
For a team-specific view, orient each margin yjiy_{ji} as team jj’s score minus its opponent’s score. Define sji=1s_{ji}=1 when team jj is home, −1-1 when away, and 00 at a neutral venue. This differs from the home-oriented hgh_g above. Then
yji=θj−θk(i)+αsji+εji.
y_{ji}=\theta_j-\theta_{k(i)}+\alpha s_{ji}+\varepsilon_{ji}.

Holding the opponent ratings and home advantage fixed, define
aji=yji+θk(i)−αsji.
a_{ji}=y_{ji}+\theta_{k(i)}-\alpha s_{ji}.

Each ajia_{ji} measures θj\theta_j with Gaussian noise. Completing the square gives the conditional posterior
θj∣other ratings, data,α,σ2,τ2∼N(∑iajiG+λ,σ2G+λ).
\theta_j\mid\text{other ratings, data},\alpha,\sigma^2,\tau^2
\sim N\!\left(
\frac{\sum_i a_{ji}}{G+\lambda},
\frac{\sigma^2}{G+\lambda}
\right).

At the joint ridge solution, the same coordinate equation uses estimated opponent ratings and α̂\hat\alpha. Against approximately average opponents, θk(i)≈0\theta_{k(i)}\approx0. Write mi=yji−α̂sjim_i=y_{ji}-\hat\alpha s_{ji} and m‾j=G−1∑imi\bar m_j=G^{-1}\sum_i m_i. The simplified objective is
Qj(θj)=∑i=1G(mi−θj)2+λθj2.
Q_j(\theta_j)=\sum_{i=1}^G(m_i-\theta_j)^2+\lambda\theta_j^2.

Its derivative gives
−2∑imi+2Gθ̂j+2λθ̂j=0,θ̂j≈GG+λm‾j.
-2\sum_i m_i+2G\hat\theta_j+2\lambda\hat\theta_j=0,
\qquad
\boxed{\hat\theta_j\approx\frac{G}{G+\lambda}\bar m_j.}

The algebra is exact for the simplified objective. The approximation is ignoring the opponents’ nonzero ratings in the full schedule. A home win by 10 points against an opponent rated 4, with home advantage 3, gives an adjusted performance of 10+4−3=1110+4-3=11. The same win away gives 10+4+3=1710+4+3=17.


4.2 What does retaining 71% of the deviation mean?
With σ=13\sigma=13 and τ=5\tau=5, λ=169/25=6.76\lambda=169/25=6.76. Using the rounded λ≈6.8\lambda\approx6.8 gives
1717+6.8≈0.714.
\frac{17}{17+6.8}\approx0.714.

Thus an adjusted average margin of +10+10 becomes a rating of about +7.1+7.1, and −10-10 becomes about −7.1-7.1. The estimate retains about 71% of the observed distance from zero and shrinks the remaining 29% toward the average-team rating. This is neither a standard deviation nor a probability of winning. More games reduce shrinkage; larger game noise or a tighter prior increase it.





lambda_grid <- c(0.001, 2, 7, 20, 60)
ridge_table <- sapply(lambda_grid, function(lambda) ridge_ratings(games_2023, lambda)$ratings)
colnames(ridge_table) <- paste0("lambda_", lambda_grid)

4.3 Estimating the variances
Rather than choose λ\lambda by hand, estimate τ2\tau^2 and σ2\sigma^2 by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the margins after integrating the ratings out,
𝒚−α𝒉∼N(𝟎,τ2XX𝖳+σ2I).
\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h\sim N\!\left(\mathbf 0,\ \tau^2XX^{\mathsf T}+\sigma^2I\right).

This is what a multilevel model does.






NoteMathematical details: integrating out the ratings





Set 𝒛=𝒚−α𝒉\mathbf z=\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h. The marginal density averages the conditional density over all possible ratings:
p(𝒛∣τ2,σ2)=∫ℝJp(𝒛∣𝜽,σ2)p(𝜽∣τ2)d𝜽.
p(\mathbf z\mid\tau^2,\sigma^2)
=\int_{\mathbb R^J}
p(\mathbf z\mid\boldsymbol\theta,\sigma^2)
p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\tau^2)\,d\boldsymbol\theta.

This is the law of total probability. Generating 𝒛\mathbf z by first drawing ratings and then drawing game noise is equivalent to forming 𝒛=X𝜽+𝜺\mathbf z=X\boldsymbol\theta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon. Linear transformations and sums of independent Gaussian variables are Gaussian, so
E(𝒛)=𝟎,Var⁡(𝒛)=τ2XX𝖳+σ2I=:V,𝒛∼N(𝟎,V).
E(\mathbf z)=\mathbf0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf z)=\tau^2XX^{\mathsf T}+\sigma^2I=:V,
\qquad \boxed{\mathbf z\sim N(\mathbf0,V).}

This evaluates the integral using a Gaussian identity. Knowing the mean and covariance is sufficient because we have already established that the distribution is Gaussian. For a scalar example, θ∼N(0,4)\theta\sim N(0,4) and z∣θ∼N(θ,9)z\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,9) imply z∼N(0,13)z\sim N(0,13): the two independent sources of variance add. Integrating out ratings retains their uncertainty; it does not set them to zero.
For an explicit calculation, let nn be the number of games and define
A=X𝖳Xσ2+Iτ2,𝒃=X𝖳𝒛σ2.
A=\frac{X^{\mathsf T}X}{\sigma^2}+\frac{I}{\tau^2},
\qquad \mathbf b=\frac{X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf z}{\sigma^2}.

The exponent in the product of the two Gaussian densities can be written as
∥𝒛−X𝜽∥2σ2+∥𝜽∥2τ2=(𝜽−A−1𝒃)𝖳A(𝜽−A−1𝒃)+𝒛𝖳𝒛σ2−𝒃𝖳A−1𝒃.
\frac{\|\mathbf z-X\boldsymbol\theta\|^2}{\sigma^2}
+\frac{\|\boldsymbol\theta\|^2}{\tau^2}
=(\boldsymbol\theta-A^{-1}\mathbf b)^{\mathsf T}
A(\boldsymbol\theta-A^{-1}\mathbf b)
+\frac{\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf z}{\sigma^2}
-\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}\mathbf b.

Use the Gaussian integral
∫ℝJexp⁡[−12(𝜽−A−1𝒃)𝖳A(𝜽−A−1𝒃)]d𝜽=(2π)J/2|A|−1/2.
\int_{\mathbb R^J}
\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(\boldsymbol\theta-A^{-1}\mathbf b)^{\mathsf T}
A(\boldsymbol\theta-A^{-1}\mathbf b)\right]d\boldsymbol\theta
=(2\pi)^{J/2}|A|^{-1/2}.

Including the original normalizing constants, the marginal density becomes
(2π)−n/2(σ2)−n/2(τ2)−J/2|A|−1/2exp⁡[−12(𝒛𝖳𝒛σ2−𝒃𝖳A−1𝒃)].
(2\pi)^{-n/2}(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}(\tau^2)^{-J/2}|A|^{-1/2}
\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12\left(
\frac{\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf z}{\sigma^2}
-\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}\mathbf b\right)\right].

This is the N(𝟎,V)N(\mathbf0,V) density. Consequently the marginal log likelihood is
ℓ(α,τ2,σ2)=−12[nlog(2π)+log|V|+(𝒚−α𝒉)𝖳V−1(𝒚−α𝒉)].
\ell(\alpha,\tau^2,\sigma^2)
=-\tfrac12\left[n\log(2\pi)+\log|V|
+(\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(\mathbf y-\alpha\mathbf h)\right].

Maximizing it estimates home advantage and both variances, giving λ̂=σ̂2/τ̂2\hat\lambda=\hat\sigma^2/\hat\tau^2.



The calculation below uses the matrix determinant lemma and the Woodbury identity so that only 32×3232\times32 matrices are inverted.

home <- 1 - games_2023$neutral_site
XtX <- crossprod(X)
J <- ncol(X)
G <- nrow(X)

marginal_log_likelihood <- function(parameters) {
  alpha <- parameters[[1]]
  tau2 <- exp(2 * parameters[[2]])
  sigma2 <- exp(2 * parameters[[3]])
  r <- games_2023$margin - alpha * home
  Xtr <- crossprod(X, r)
  inner <- XtX + (sigma2 / tau2) * diag(J)
  log_det <- (G - J) * log(sigma2) + as.numeric(determinant(sigma2 * diag(J) + tau2 * XtX)$modulus)
  quadratic <- (sum(r^2) - as.numeric(t(Xtr) %*% solve(inner, Xtr))) / sigma2
  -0.5 * (log_det + quadratic + G * log(2 * pi))
}

ml_fit <- optim(c(2, log(5), log(13)), function(p) -marginal_log_likelihood(p), method = "BFGS")

alpha_hat <- ml_fit$par[[1]]
tau_hat <- exp(ml_fit$par[[2]])
sigma_hat <- exp(ml_fit$par[[3]])
lambda_hat <- sigma_hat^2 / tau_hat^2

  tau = tau_hat,
  sigma = sigma_hat,
  lambda = lambda_hat,

text:
6 Held-out evaluation
Fit on weeks 1 through 14 and predict weeks 15 through 18. Turn each predicted margin into a home-win probability with the fitted noise scale,
P(home wins)=Φ(α̂hg+θ̂home−θ̂awayσ̂).
P(\text{home wins})=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\hat\alpha h_g+\hat\theta_{\text{home}}-\hat\theta_{\text{away}}}{\hat\sigma}\right).







NoteWhy divide by the fitted noise scale?



Dividing by σ̂\hat\sigma expresses the predicted margin in standard deviations, because Φ\Phi is the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal random variable.
Write the predicted home-team margin as μ̂g=α̂hg+θ̂home−θ̂away\hat\mu_g=\hat\alpha h_g+\hat\theta_{\text{home}}-\hat\theta_{\text{away}}. Under the fitted model,
Mg=μ̂g+εg,εg∼N(0,σ̂2).
M_g=\hat\mu_g+\varepsilon_g,\qquad \varepsilon_g\sim N(0,\hat\sigma^2).

The home team wins when Mg>0M_g>0. Standardizing the noise gives
P(Mg>0)=P(εgσ̂>−μ̂gσ̂)=1−Φ(−μ̂gσ̂)=Φ(μ̂gσ̂),
P(M_g>0)
=P\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon_g}{\hat\sigma}>-\frac{\hat\mu_g}{\hat\sigma}\right)
=1-\Phi\!\left(-\frac{\hat\mu_g}{\hat\sigma}\right)
=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\hat\mu_g}{\hat\sigma}\right),

where the last equality uses the symmetry of the standard normal distribution. Here σ̂\hat\sigma estimates the game-to-game noise standard deviation around the expected margin.
For example, a predicted 7-point advantage with σ̂=14\hat\sigma=14 is a 7/14=0.57/14=0.5-standard-deviation advantage, giving Φ(0.5)≈0.69\Phi(0.5)\approx0.69, or about a 69% chance of winning. More game-to-game noise means the same predicted advantage gives less certainty of a win.



train <- games_2023 %>% filter(week <= 14)
test <- games_2023 %>% filter(week >= 15, tie == 0)

# Reestimate every tuning and noise parameter using training games only.
train_hyper <- fit_margin_hyperparameters(train)
sigma_train <- train_hyper$sigma
lambda_train <- train_hyper$lambda

predict_margin <- function(ratings, home_advantage, games) {
  home_advantage * (1 - games$neutral_site) + ratings[games$home_team] - ratings[games$away_team]
}

evaluate <- function(ratings, home_advantage, label) {
  predicted <- predict_margin(ratings, home_advantage, test)
  probability <- pnorm(predicted / sigma_train)
  data.frame(
    model = label,
    rmse_margin = sqrt(mean((test$margin - predicted)^2)),
    log_loss = log_loss(test$home_win, probability),
    brier = brier_score(test$home_win, probability)
  )
}

massey_train <- massey_ratings(train)
ridge_train <- ridge_ratings(train, lambda_train)
ridge_strong <- ridge_ratings(train, 4 * lambda_train)

bind_rows(
  evaluate(setNames(rep(0, J), colnames(X)), train_hyper$home_advantage, "home advantage only"),
  evaluate(massey_train$ratings, massey_train$home_advantage, "least squares"),

Game outcomes fit a regression with one ±1\pm1 column per team and a home-field term; least squares gives schedule-adjusted ratings.

title: Lecture 5: Team Performance Evaluation
text:
How strong is a team, and how sure are we?
A win-loss record answers neither question well. It ignores margins, it ignores who the opponents were, and over a 17-game NFL season or a 38-match Premier League season it contains a great deal of luck. This lecture builds team ratings that address each problem in turn:

Regression ratings explain game margins with one parameter per team plus a home advantage, which adjusts for schedule automatically.
A Gaussian prior on the ratings, the same idea as ridge regression and the multilevel models of Lecture 4, controls the noise in a short season.
Bradley-Terry models rate teams from wins and losses alone, and the Elo system turns out to be an online version of the same model.
A Bayesian multilevel Poisson model treats soccer goals as counts with attack and defense effects and produces full match-outcome probabilities.
State-space models let strength change over time, and the Kalman filter connects Elo’s update rule to Bayesian sequential updating.
Forecast evaluation compares every rating system with the betting market and reports rankings with their uncertainty.

2 Strength is latent; outcomes are observed
Let θj\theta_j denote the strength of team jj: the expected margin against an average opponent on a neutral field. No game reveals θj\theta_j directly. Every rating system in this lecture is a rule for turning those outcomes into estimates of θ\theta, and every one of them has to deal with three facts.

Outcomes are noisy. A single NFL game has a margin standard deviation near 14 points around its expectation.
Schedules differ. A team’s results depend on who it played.
Home matters. The home team wins more often than not in every major league.

text:
4 Talent and luck
Treat each team’s season win percentage as a noisy measurement of its true winning probability pjp_j:
WP̂j=pj+ej,E[ej∣pj]=0,Var⁡(ej∣pj)=pj(1−pj)G,
\widehat{\mathrm{WP}}_j=p_j+e_j,
\qquad
E[e_j\mid p_j]=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e_j\mid p_j)=\frac{p_j(1-p_j)}{G},

where GG is the number of games. This assumes independent, tie-free games with a constant win probability for each team. Across the league, the law of total variance gives
Var⁡(WP̂)=Var⁡(p)⏟talent+E[p(1−p)]G⏟luck.
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\mathrm{WP}}\right)
=\underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(p)}_{\text{talent}}
+\underbrace{\frac{E[p(1-p)]}{G}}_{\text{luck}}.

The exact luck variance under this model is obtained by averaging the conditional variance across teams. Since E[e∣p]=0E[e\mid p]=0 and E[p2]=Var⁡(p)+p‾2E[p^2]=\operatorname{Var}(p)+\bar p^2, where p‾=E[p]\bar p=E[p],
Var⁡(e)=E[Var⁡(e∣p)]+Var⁡(E[e∣p])=E[p]−E[p2]G=p‾(1−p‾)−Var⁡(p)G.
\operatorname{Var}(e)
=E[\operatorname{Var}(e\mid p)]+\operatorname{Var}(E[e\mid p])
=\frac{E[p]-E[p^2]}{G}
=\frac{\bar p(1-\bar p)-\operatorname{Var}(p)}{G}.

For a simple approximation, neglect the Var⁡(p)\operatorname{Var}(p) term in this numerator. With p‾=0.5\bar p=0.5, luck variance is then approximately 0.25/G0.25/G. This is the signal-plus-noise decomposition of Lecture 4 applied to teams: subtract the approximate luck variance from the observed variance to estimate talent variance. The calculation below treats season length as 17 games; actual ties, unequal schedules, and shared games make this an illustrative decomposition.

luck_variance <- 0.25 / 17  # Approximation, not the exact binomial mixture variance.
observed_variance <- var(standings$win_pct)
talent_variance <- observed_variance - luck_variance

data.frame(
  observed_variance = observed_variance,
  approximate_luck_variance = luck_variance,
  estimated_talent_variance = talent_variance,
  talent_share = talent_variance / observed_variance,
  games_for_equal_share = 0.25 / talent_variance
) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)

Roughly 40% of the variance in NFL records over these three seasons is attributed to luck by this approximation, and talent and luck contribute equally at about twelve games, so a 17-game season is only modestly more signal than noise. The same reasoning gives the approximate linear shrinkage estimate of a team’s true winning probability,
p̂j=p‾+Var⁡(p)Var⁡(p)+p‾(1−p‾)/G(WP̂j−p‾),
\hat p_j=\bar p+\frac{\operatorname{Var}(p)}{\operatorname{Var}(p)+\bar p(1-\bar p)/G}\left(\widehat{\mathrm{WP}}_j-\bar p\right),

which regresses every record toward .500 by a factor equal to the approximate talent share. Here the variance components are replaced by their estimates above.

text:
5 Schedules
A team’s average margin also depends on whom it played. Define the naive rating as the average margin,
rj(0)=1Gj∑g∈𝒢j(points for−points against)g.
r_j^{(0)}=\frac{1}{G_j}\sum_{g\in\mathcal G_j}\left(\text{points for}-\text{points against}\right)_g.

A fair rating should add back the quality of the opposition: a team that averages +3+3 against opponents who are themselves +2+2 is better than a team that averages +3+3 against opponents who are −2-2. That suggests the iteration
rj(t+1)=1Gj∑g∈𝒢j[marging+ropp(g)(t)],
r_j^{(t+1)}=\frac{1}{G_j}\sum_{g\in\mathcal G_j}\left[\text{margin}_g+r^{(t)}_{\text{opp}(g)}\right],

which repeatedly adjusts each rating by the average current rating of its opponents.

games_2023 <- nfl %>% filter(season == 2023)
teams <- sort(unique(games_2023$home_team))

long <- bind_rows(
  games_2023 %>% transmute(team = home_team, opponent = away_team, margin = margin),
  games_2023 %>% transmute(team = away_team, opponent = home_team, margin = -margin)
)

rating <- setNames(rep(0, length(teams)), teams)
for (iteration in seq_len(50)) {
  rating <- long %>%
    mutate(opponent_rating = rating[opponent]) %>%
    group_by(team) %>%
    summarize(rating = mean(margin + opponent_rating), .groups = "drop") %>%
    with(setNames(rating, team))
  rating <- rating - mean(rating)
}

7 Practice

A team goes 12-5 with a point differential of +20+20. Explain in one sentence why its Pythagorean record is far below 12-5.
Using the talent variance estimated above, what is the shrinkage estimate of true winning probability for a 13-4 team?

A +20+20 differential over 17 games is about +1.2+1.2 per game, which corresponds to only slightly better than a .500 team; the 12-5 record came from winning close games.

title: 5.1 Team Evaluation: Outcomes, Luck, and Schedules
text:
8 Key takeaways

Team strength is latent; outcomes are noisy functions of strength differences plus home advantage.
Point differential carries more information than the record and predicts future records at least as well.
Roughly 40% of the variance in NFL records is attributed to luck by the simple approximation; shrink records toward .500 accordingly.
Schedule adjustment is a system of equations, one per team, which is a regression in disguise.
Soccer needs count models and a third outcome.

text:
2 The Bradley-Terry model
Assign each team a positive strength πj\pi_j and let
P(i beats j)=πiπi+πj.
P(i\text{ beats }j)=\frac{\pi_i}{\pi_i+\pi_j}.

Writing θj=log⁡πj\theta_j=\log\pi_j gives
P(i beats j)=eθieθi+eθj=σ(θi−θj),
P(i\text{ beats }j)=\frac{e^{\theta_i}}{e^{\theta_i}+e^{\theta_j}}=\sigma(\theta_i-\theta_j),

where σ\sigma is the logistic function. The probability depends only on the difference in ratings, so a constant can be added to every θj\theta_j without changing anything: the same identification issue as in Tutorial 5.2, resolved the same way.
With a home advantage α\alpha and the design matrix XX of Tutorial 5.2,
P(home wins game g)=σ(αhg+∑jxgjθj),
P(\text{home wins game }g)=\sigma\!\left(\alpha h_g+\sum_j x_{gj}\theta_j\right),

which is a logistic regression with no intercept, one column for home field, and the ±1\pm1 team columns. Everything we know about logistic regression applies: the log-likelihood
ℓ(α,𝜽)=∑g[yglogpg+(1−yg)log(1−pg)]
\ell(\alpha,\boldsymbol\theta)=\sum_g\left[y_g\log p_g+(1-y_g)\log(1-p_g)\right]

is concave, maximum likelihood is a standard glm() call, and the coefficients are log-odds.

2.1 Fit on the 2023 NFL season

text:
4 Elo is an online Bradley-Terry model
The Elo system computes the expected score of team ii against team jj as
Ei=11+10−(Ri−Rj)/400,
E_i=\frac{1}{1+10^{-(R_i-R_j)/400}},

and after the game updates Ri←Ri+K(Si−Ei)R_i\leftarrow R_i+K(S_i-E_i), where SiS_i is 1 for a win, 0 for a loss, and 0.5 for a tie.
Two facts connect this to the model above.
The expected score is a Bradley-Terry probability. Since 10−x/400=e−xln⁡10/40010^{-x/400}=e^{-x\ln10/400},
Ei=σ(ln⁡10400(Ri−Rj)),
E_i=\sigma\!\left(\frac{\ln 10}{400}(R_i-R_j)\right),

so θj=Rjln⁡10/400\theta_j=R_j\ln10/400. An Elo gap of 400 points is a rating difference of about 2.3 log-odds, or a 91% win probability.
The update is a gradient step. The derivative of one game’s log-likelihood with respect to θi\theta_i is
∂∂θi[ylogp+(1−y)log(1−p)]=y−p,
\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_i}\left[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)\right]=y-p,

where p=σ(θi−θj)p=\sigma(\theta_i-\theta_j). The Elo update adds K(Si−Ei)K(S_i-E_i), which is a step of size KK along that gradient. Elo is therefore stochastic gradient ascent on the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood, processing one game at a time and never revisiting old games. The constant KK controls how fast ratings respond, and Tutorial 5.5 shows that it plays the same role as the innovation variance of a state-space model.

6 Held-out comparison
Fit the Bradley-Terry and margin models on weeks 1 through 14 of 2023 and score their home-win probabilities on weeks 15 through 18. To avoid the separation problem in the training window, the Bradley-Terry fit uses a mild ridge penalty implemented as the posterior mode with τ=1\tau=1.

train <- games_2023 %>% filter(week <= 14, tie == 0)
test <- games_2023 %>% filter(week >= 15, tie == 0)
X_train <- build_design_matrix(train, teams = colnames(X))
X_test <- build_design_matrix(test, teams = colnames(X))

# Penalized logistic regression by Newton's method: the posterior mode with
# a N(0, tau^2) prior on every team rating and a N(0, 3^2) prior on home field.
penalized_logistic <- function(A, y, prior_sd) {
  beta <- rep(0, ncol(A))
  penalty <- diag(1 / prior_sd^2)
  for (iteration in seq_len(50)) {
    p <- plogis(as.numeric(A %*% beta))
    gradient <- as.numeric(t(A) %*% (y - p)) - penalty %*% beta
    hessian <- t(A) %*% (A * (p * (1 - p))) + penalty
    step <- solve(hessian, gradient)
    beta <- beta + as.numeric(step)
    if (max(abs(step)) < 1e-8) break
  }
  beta
}

A_train <- cbind(home = 1 - train$neutral_site, X_train)
bt_beta <- penalized_logistic(A_train, train$home_win, prior_sd = c(3, rep(1, ncol(X_train))))
bt_probability <- plogis(as.numeric(cbind(1 - test$neutral_site, X_test) %*% bt_beta))

margin_train <- ridge_ratings(train, lambda = 7)
margin_prediction <- margin_train$home_advantage * (1 - test$neutral_site) +
  margin_train$ratings[test$home_team] - margin_train$ratings[test$away_team]
margin_probability <- pnorm(margin_prediction / 13)

data.frame(
  model = c("Bradley-Terry (penalized)", "ridge on margins"),
  log_loss = c(log_loss(test$home_win, bt_probability), log_loss(test$home_win, margin_probability)),
  brier = c(brier_score(test$home_win, bt_probability), brier_score(test$home_win, margin_probability))

8 Key takeaways

Bradley-Terry is logistic regression on the ±1\pm1 design; ratings are log-odds.
Undefeated teams break maximum likelihood; a normal prior restores finite, interpretable ratings.
Elo’s expected score is a Bradley-Terry probability and its update is a gradient step with step size KK.
Ordered-outcome models handle draws with thresholds on the latent scale.
Margin models extract more information per game; win-loss models are for when margins are unavailable or untrustworthy.

2 Why static ratings are not enough
Every model so far assigns one rating per team per season and treats week 1 and week 18 as equally informative about the team today. Strength changes: quarterbacks get hurt, rosters turn over, and between seasons the changes are larger still. A rating that is supposed to describe a team now should weight recent games more heavily, and it should carry uncertainty that grows when the team has not played.

3 The Elo system
Elo maintains a rating RjR_j for each team and updates it after every game. For a game between home team ii and away team jj with home advantage AA rating points,
Ei=11+10−(Ri+A−Rj)/400,Ri←Ri+K(Si−Ei),Rj←Rj−K(Si−Ei),
E_i=\frac{1}{1+10^{-(R_i+A-R_j)/400}},
\qquad
R_i\leftarrow R_i+K(S_i-E_i),
\qquad
R_j\leftarrow R_j-K(S_i-E_i),

where SiS_i is 1 for a home win, 0 for a loss, and 0.5 for a tie. Tutorial 5.3 showed that EiE_i is a Bradley-Terry probability and that the update is a gradient step of size KK. Two further conventions are common.

Season regression. Before each new season, every rating is moved a fraction rr of the way back toward the starting value: Rj←Rj+r(1500−Rj)R_j\leftarrow R_j+r(1500-R_j). This encodes the belief that rosters change.

text:
4 A state-space model for strength
Elo’s update is a rule; a state-space model is a probability model whose optimal update we can derive. Following Glickman and Stern (1998), let θj,t\theta_{j,t} be team jj’s strength in period tt (one NFL week) and let strengths evolve as a random walk:
θj,t=θj,t−1+ωj,t,ωj,t∼N(0,σw2).
\theta_{j,t}=\theta_{j,t-1}+\omega_{j,t},
\qquad
\omega_{j,t}\sim N(0,\sigma_w^2).

Between seasons the change is larger and includes regression toward the mean:
θj,first week=ρθj,last week+vj,vj∼N(0,σs2),0<ρ<1.
\theta_{j,\text{first week}}=\rho\,\theta_{j,\text{last week}}+v_j,
\qquad
v_j\sim N(0,\sigma_s^2),
\qquad
0<\rho<1.

Each game observes a noisy difference of current strengths:
yg=θhome(g),t−θaway(g),t+h⋅homeg+εg,εg∼N(0,σ2).
y_g=\theta_{\text{home}(g),t}-\theta_{\text{away}(g),t}+h\cdot\text{home}_g+\varepsilon_g,
\qquad
\varepsilon_g\sim N(0,\sigma^2).

The model has four variances and two constants: σ2\sigma^2 (game noise), σw2\sigma_w^2 (weekly drift), σs2\sigma_s^2 (between-season change), the initial spread, ρ\rho, and hh. Each has a direct meaning, which is the advantage over Elo’s KK.

4.1 The Kalman filter
Because every distribution is normal and every relationship is linear, the posterior of the strength vector 𝜽t\boldsymbol\theta_t given all games through period tt is normal, N(𝒎t,Pt)N(\mathbf m_t,P_t), and it can be updated in closed form. Write 𝑯g\mathbf H_g for the vector with +1+1 at the home team, −1-1 at the away team, and zeros elsewhere.
Predict (move to the next period):
𝒎t−=𝒎t−1,Pt−=Pt−1+σw2I.
\mathbf m_t^{-}=\mathbf m_{t-1},
\qquad
P_t^{-}=P_{t-1}+\sigma_w^2 I.

Update (observe game gg):
ŷg=𝑯g𝖳𝒎+h⋅homeg,Sg=𝑯g𝖳P𝑯g+σ2,𝒌g=P𝑯gSg,
\hat y_g=\mathbf H_g^{\mathsf T}\mathbf m+h\cdot\text{home}_g,
\qquad
S_g=\mathbf H_g^{\mathsf T}P\mathbf H_g+\sigma^2,
\qquad
\mathbf k_g=\frac{P\mathbf H_g}{S_g},

𝒎←𝒎+𝒌g(yg−ŷg),P←P−𝒌g𝑯g𝖳P.
\mathbf m\leftarrow\mathbf m+\mathbf k_g\left(y_g-\hat y_g\right),
\qquad
P\leftarrow P-\mathbf k_g\mathbf H_g^{\mathsf T}P.

The update is prediction error times a gain 𝒌g\mathbf k_g. The gain is large when the current uncertainty PP is large relative to the game noise σ2\sigma^2 and small when the ratings are already well established. This is Bayesian sequential updating: the posterior after each game is the prior for the next, exactly as in the beta-binomial example of Lecture 4, but with the drift step adding uncertainty between periods.






NoteShow derivation: Kalman prediction and update





The filter repeats two steps: predict the current strength distribution, then update it using the new result. We derive both below, following the scalar-to-vector approach in the accompanying study notes.

4.1.1 1. Prediction: carry the previous posterior forward
Let 𝒟t−1\mathcal D_{t-1} denote all results through the previous week. Suppose the strength vector after those results has distribution
𝜽t−1∣𝒟t−1∼N(𝒎t−1,Pt−1).
\boldsymbol\theta_{t-1}\mid\mathcal D_{t-1}
\sim N(\mathbf m_{t-1},P_{t-1}).

Here 𝒎t−1\mathbf m_{t-1} contains the estimated team strengths, and Pt−1P_{t-1} contains their variances and covariances. Start the first week with a normal prior, such as N(𝟎,σinitial2I)N(\mathbf0,\sigma_{\mathrm{initial}}^2I). For this derivation, treat the home advantage and noise variances as fixed. Assume the initial state, state innovations, and game errors are mutually independent, with independent noise across periods and games.
The weekly state equation is
𝜽t=𝜽t−1+𝝎t,𝝎t∼N(𝟎,σw2I).
\boldsymbol\theta_t=\boldsymbol\theta_{t-1}+\boldsymbol\omega_t,
\qquad \boldsymbol\omega_t\sim N(\mathbf0,\sigma_w^2I).

Take the conditional expectation of both sides. The new innovation has mean zero and is independent of the previous results, so
𝒎t−=E[𝜽t∣𝒟t−1]=E[𝜽t−1∣𝒟t−1]+E[𝝎t∣𝒟t−1]=𝒎t−1.
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf m_t^-
&=E[\boldsymbol\theta_t\mid\mathcal D_{t-1}]\\
&=E[\boldsymbol\theta_{t-1}\mid\mathcal D_{t-1}]
  +E[\boldsymbol\omega_t\mid\mathcal D_{t-1}]\\
&=\boxed{\mathbf m_{t-1}}.
\end{aligned}

Independence also makes the cross-covariance terms zero. Therefore
Pt−=Var⁡(𝜽t∣𝒟t−1)=Var⁡(𝜽t−1∣𝒟t−1)+Var⁡(𝝎t)=Pt−1+σw2I.
\begin{aligned}
P_t^-&=\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\theta_t\mid\mathcal D_{t-1})\\
&=\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\theta_{t-1}\mid\mathcal D_{t-1})
 +\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\omega_t)\\
&=\boxed{P_{t-1}+\sigma_w^2I}.
\end{aligned}

A sum of independent normal vectors is normal, giving 𝜽t∣𝒟t−1∼N(𝒎t−,Pt−)\boldsymbol\theta_t\mid\mathcal D_{t-1}\sim N(\mathbf m_t^-,P_t^-). The minus sign means before the current observations. Time leaves expected strength unchanged but increases uncertainty. This is prediction through the state equation, not yet a Bayes update.
At a season boundary the equation is instead 𝜽new=ρ𝜽old+𝝂\boldsymbol\theta_{\mathrm{new}}=\rho\boldsymbol\theta_{\mathrm{old}}+
\boldsymbol\nu, with independent 𝝂∼N(𝟎,σs2I)\boldsymbol\nu\sim N(\mathbf0,\sigma_s^2I). The same reasoning gives
𝒎new−=ρ𝒎old,Pnew−=ρ2Pold+σs2I.
\boxed{\mathbf m_{\mathrm{new}}^-=\rho\mathbf m_{\mathrm{old}}},
\qquad
\boxed{P_{\mathrm{new}}^-=\rho^2P_{\mathrm{old}}+\sigma_s^2I}.

The mean is multiplied by ρ\rho, while the covariance is multiplied by ρ2\rho^2, because variances scale quadratically.


4.1.2 2. Update in one dimension: multiply the prior by the likelihood
First consider just one unknown strength and one measurement:
θ∣𝒟∼N(m,P),Y∣θ,𝒟∼N(θ,r),P,r>0.
\theta\mid\mathcal D\sim N(m,P),\qquad
Y\mid\theta,\mathcal D\sim N(\theta,r),\qquad P,r>0.

Here 𝒟\mathcal D is the information already incorporated, PP is the prior variance, and rr is the measurement-error variance. Bayes’ rule is
p(θ∣y,𝒟)=p(y∣θ,𝒟)p(θ∣𝒟)p(y∣𝒟)∝p(y∣θ,𝒟)p(θ∣𝒟).
p(\theta\mid y,\mathcal D)
=\frac{p(y\mid\theta,\mathcal D)p(\theta\mid\mathcal D)}
       {p(y\mid\mathcal D)}
\propto p(y\mid\theta,\mathcal D)p(\theta\mid\mathcal D).

The denominator does not depend on the candidate θ\theta, so it can be absorbed into a normalizing constant. Substituting the two normal densities,
p(θ∣y,𝒟)∝exp⁡[−12{(θ−m)2P+(y−θ)2r}].
p(\theta\mid y,\mathcal D)\propto
\exp\left[-\frac12\left\{
\frac{(\theta-m)^2}{P}+\frac{(y-\theta)^2}{r}\right\}\right].

Expand the expression in braces and collect powers of θ\theta:
(1P+1r)θ2−2(mP+yr)θ+C,
\left(\frac1P+\frac1r\right)\theta^2
-2\left(\frac mP+\frac yr\right)\theta+C,

where CC does not depend on θ\theta. Define
P+=(1P+1r)−1=PrP+r,m+=P+(mP+yr)=rm+PyP+r.
P^+=\left(\frac1P+\frac1r\right)^{-1}=\frac{Pr}{P+r},
\qquad
m^+=P^+\left(\frac mP+\frac yr\right)
=\frac{rm+Py}{P+r}.

Completing the square gives (θ−m+)2/P++C′(\theta-m^+)^2/P^++C'. Thus the posterior is N(m+,P+)N(m^+,P^+). Set K=P/(P+r)K=P/(P+r) and rearrange:
m+=m+K(y−m),P+=(1−K)P.
\boxed{m^+=m+K(y-m)},\qquad
\boxed{P^+=(1-K)P}.

The posterior mean is (1−K)m+Ky(1-K)m+Ky: a weighted average of the prior mean and the observation. Larger prior uncertainty gives more weight to the new result; larger measurement noise gives less. A normal prior and likelihood together, not normal observation noise alone, produce the normal posterior. This is why prediction and updating preserve normality when we start from a normal initial state.


4.1.3 3. Update for teams: a game measures a strength difference
Immediately before game gg, write 𝜽∣𝒟∼N(𝒎,P)\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D\sim N(\mathbf m,P). These are the current values, including any games already processed this week. Let HgH_g have +1 for the home team, -1 for the away team, and zero elsewhere:
Yg=HgT𝜽+hhomeg+εg,εg∼N(0,σ2).
Y_g=H_g^T\boldsymbol\theta+h\,\mathrm{home}_g+\varepsilon_g,
\qquad \varepsilon_g\sim N(0,\sigma^2).

With the venue and model parameters fixed, taking expectation and variance gives the predicted margin and its variance:
ŷg=E[Yg∣𝒟]=HgT𝒎+hhomeg,
\hat y_g=E[Y_g\mid\mathcal D]
=H_g^T\mathbf m+h\,\mathrm{home}_g,
 Sg=Var⁡(Yg∣𝒟)=HgTPHg+σ2.
S_g=\operatorname{Var}(Y_g\mid\mathcal D)
=H_g^TPH_g+\sigma^2.

The strength–observation covariance follows from independence of the observation error:
Cov⁡(𝜽,Yg∣𝒟)=Cov⁡(𝜽,HgT𝜽+εg∣𝒟)=PHg.
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\theta,Y_g\mid\mathcal D)
=\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\theta,H_g^T\boldsymbol\theta+
\varepsilon_g\mid\mathcal D)=PH_g.

The state and observation are jointly normal, with
(𝜽Yg)∣𝒟∼N((𝒎ŷg),(PPHgHgTPSg)).
\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\theta\\Y_g\end{pmatrix}\mid\mathcal D
\sim N\left(
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf m\\\hat y_g\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}P&PH_g\\H_g^TP&S_g\end{pmatrix}
\right).

The vector version of completing the square uses the conditional-normal identities
E[X∣Z=z]=μX+ΣXZΣZZ−1(z−μZ),
E[X\mid Z=z]=\mu_X+\Sigma_{XZ}\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1}(z-\mu_Z),
 Var⁡(X∣Z=z)=ΣXX−ΣXZΣZZ−1ΣZX.
\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Z=z)
=\Sigma_{XX}-\Sigma_{XZ}\Sigma_{ZZ}^{-1}\Sigma_{ZX}.

Substitute X=𝜽X=\boldsymbol\theta, Z=YgZ=Y_g, ΣXZ=PHg\Sigma_{XZ}=PH_g, and ΣZZ=Sg\Sigma_{ZZ}=S_g. Because SgS_g is a scalar, its inverse is simply 1/Sg1/S_g. We obtain
𝒌g=PHgSg,𝒎+=𝒎+𝒌g(yg−ŷg),
\boxed{\mathbf k_g=\frac{PH_g}{S_g}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf m^+=\mathbf m+\mathbf k_g(y_g-\hat y_g)},
 P+=P−PHgHgTPSg=P−𝒌gHgTP.
\boxed{P^+=P-\frac{PH_gH_g^TP}{S_g}
=P-\mathbf k_gH_g^TP}.

These are the lecture’s update formulas: prediction error multiplied by a gain, followed by a reduction in uncertainty. All right-hand sides use the values before the update. In particular, if the home and away teams are AA and BB,
HgTPHg=PAA+PBB−2PAB,kg,j=PjA−PjBPAA+PBB−2PAB+σ2.
H_g^TPH_g=P_{AA}+P_{BB}-2P_{AB},\qquad
k_{g,j}=\frac{P_{jA}-P_{jB}}
{P_{AA}+P_{BB}-2P_{AB}+\sigma^2}.

The covariance term matters: team strengths need not remain independent once game results have been incorporated.


4.1.4 4. A numerical example
Use the values from the study notes:
𝒎=(4−1),P=(90016),Hg=(1−1),h=3,homeg=1,σ2=100.
\mathbf m=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
P=\begin{pmatrix}9&0\\0&16\end{pmatrix},\quad
H_g=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
h=3,\quad\mathrm{home}_g=1,\quad\sigma^2=100.

The predicted margin is ŷg=4−(−1)+3=8\hat y_g=4-(-1)+3=8. Suppose the home team wins by 18, so the prediction error is 10. Then
Sg=9+16+100=125,𝒌g=1125(9−16)=(0.072−0.128),
S_g=9+16+100=125,\qquad
\mathbf k_g=\frac1{125}\begin{pmatrix}9\\-16\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0.072\\-0.128\end{pmatrix},
 𝒎+=(4−1)+(0.072−0.128)10=(4.72−2.28),
\mathbf m^+=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\end{pmatrix}
+\begin{pmatrix}0.072\\-0.128\end{pmatrix}10
=\begin{pmatrix}4.72\\-2.28\end{pmatrix},
 P+=(90016)−1125(81−144−144256)=(8.3521.1521.15213.952).
P^+=\begin{pmatrix}9&0\\0&16\end{pmatrix}
-\frac1{125}\begin{pmatrix}81&-144\\-144&256\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}8.352&1.152\\1.152&13.952\end{pmatrix}.

The away team moves more because its prior variance was larger. Both individual variances decrease, and the variance of the strength difference falls from 25 to 8.352+13.952−2(1.152)=208.352+13.952-2(1.152)=20.
For several games in the same week, use each updated distribution as the prior for the next game. Add weekly drift only when moving to a new week, not after every game. The recurring sequence is:
Previous posterior → predict through the state equation → current prior → observe a game and apply Bayes’ rule → current posterior.










NoteElo as a constant-gain filter



Elo’s update K(Si−Ei)K(S_i-E_i) has the same form, prediction error times a gain, with a constant gain KK and a binary observation. In the state-space model the gain settles to a steady value once PP stops changing, which happens when the uncertainty added by drift each week balances the uncertainty removed by each game. Elo with a well-chosen KK approximates that steady-state filter. The state-space model adds three things: a gain that starts large for new teams, an explicit uncertainty for every rating, and hyperparameters that can be estimated rather than tuned.

text:
7 Key takeaways

Elo is a constant-gain sequential update whose KK should be tuned by forecast quality; a margin multiplier improves it.
A random-walk state-space model gives every rating a time index and an uncertainty, with hyperparameters that mean something.
The Kalman filter is the exact Bayesian update for that model and reduces to an Elo-like rule with a data-driven gain.
Stan estimates the hyperparameters and yields smoothed paths; valid historical forecasts require filtering with hyperparameters chosen without future outcomes.
